summary.text: Amines are organic compounds that contain carbon–nitrogen bonds.
They form when one or more hydrogen atoms in ammonia are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
Amines are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary, and the nitrogen atom in an amine has a lone pair of electrons.

facts.label: Simplest aromatic amine
facts.value: Aniline, a benzene ring with an amino group

facts.label: Amino group
facts.value: The −NH₂ group found in primary amines

facts.label: Quaternary ammonium
facts.value: Four organic substituents on the nitrogen

items.prompt: In an amine, the nitrogen carries two carbon groups and one hydrogen. What class of amine is it?

options.label: Secondary
Primary
Tertiary
Quaternary

items.explain: Secondary amines have two alkyl or aryl groups on the nitrogen, along with one hydrogen.

items.prompt: A nitrogen compound has its nitrogen attached to a carbonyl group, R−C(=O)−NR′R″. What is it called?

options.label: A tertiary amine
An amide
A quaternary ammonium salt
A cyclic amine

items.explain: Compounds where the nitrogen is attached to a carbonyl group are called amides.

items.prompt: A student compares ethylamine with ethyl alcohol at standard conditions. What does she find?

options.label: The amine is a liquid and the alcohol is a gas
Both are solids that melt only on heating
Both are gases that look the same
The amine is a gas and the alcohol is a liquid

items.explain: Methyl and ethyl amines are gases under standard conditions, whereas the corresponding alcohols are liquids.

items.prompt: Aniline dissolves poorly in water compared with a simple small amine. What best explains this?

options.label: Its lone pair is spread into the benzene ring, so it hydrogen-bonds less
Its lone pair is missing, so it cannot bond to anything at all
Its benzene ring adds an extra charge that repels water
Its amino group is tertiary, so it has no hydrogens to share

items.explain: In aromatic amines the lone pair is conjugated into the benzene ring, which diminishes hydrogen bonding, so water solubility is low.

items.prompt: A chemist sees two N–H bands in the infrared spectrum of an amine. What does that point to?

options.label: A secondary amine
A tertiary amine
A primary amine
A quaternary ammonium salt

items.explain: Primary amines show two N–H bands in the infrared spectrum, whereas secondary amines show only one.

items.prompt: A chemist writes N- in front of a group in an amine's name. What does it show?

options.label: That the amine contains only normal, straight chains
That the group is attached to the nitrogen atom
That the compound carries a net negative charge
That the molecule has more than one nitrogen atom

items.explain: The prefix N- shows substitution on the nitrogen atom.

paragraphs.heading: What an amine is
paragraphs.text: Amines are organic compounds that contain bonds between carbon and nitrogen. You can picture one as ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been swapped for alkyl or aryl groups. The nitrogen atom in an amine carries a lone pair of electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Three classes
paragraphs.text: Amines come in three classes, set by how many groups sit on the nitrogen. A primary amine has one alkyl or aryl group, with the general formula RNH₂, and its −NH₂ part is called the amino group. A secondary amine has two such groups, R₂NH, and a tertiary amine has three, R₃N.

paragraphs.heading: Familiar examples
paragraphs.text: Methylamine, most amino acids and the buffering agent tris are important primary amines. Aniline, C₆H₇N, a benzene ring joined to an amino group, is the simplest aromatic amine. Dimethylamine is a secondary amine, and trimethylamine, a tertiary amine, has a distinctly fishy smell. Amines can also form rings, such as the three-membered aziridine and the six-membered piperidine, and these cyclic amines are either secondary or tertiary.

paragraphs.heading: Close relatives
paragraphs.text: Two related kinds of compound go by other names. If the nitrogen is attached to a carbonyl group, giving R−C(=O)−NR′R″, the compound is an amide. If the nitrogen carries four organic groups, giving R₄N⁺X⁻, the compound is a quaternary ammonium salt.

paragraphs.heading: Hydrogen bonds and smell
paragraphs.text: Hydrogen bonding strongly shapes how primary and secondary amines behave. Methyl and ethyl amines are gases at standard conditions, while methyl and ethyl alcohols are liquids. Hydrogen bonding through the lone pair also helps simple amines dissolve in water. Amines smell like ammonia, and the liquid ones have a foul, fishy odor.

paragraphs.heading: Grabbing a hydrogen ion
paragraphs.text: The lone pair on nitrogen can bind a hydrogen ion, H⁺, turning the amine into an ammonium ion, R₃NH⁺. In aromatic amines such as aniline, the lone pair is shared out into the benzene ring, so these amines form hydrogen bonds less readily. They have high boiling points and dissolve poorly in water.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting an amine
paragraphs.text: Chemists usually confirm an amine by combining mass spectrometry with NMR and IR spectroscopy. The ¹H NMR signals of an amine vanish when the sample is treated with D₂O. In an infrared spectrum, primary and secondary amines show N–H stretching bands near 3300 cm⁻¹. A primary amine gives two of these N–H bands, while a secondary amine gives only one.
